# Packaging and Install: Images, Charts, Bundles and Preflight Checks

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against Helm 3.22.1 and 4.3.1 docs, Docker CLI docs, Kubernetes docs, NVIDIA CUDA and Container Toolkit docs, skopeo docs, and a local run of the preflight script.

Builds on: containers and Kubernetes (lesson containers-ci/01-containers-from-first-principles and 03-kubernetes-for-a-service-engineer)

Scope: general concepts about packaging and installing software in a customer's environment. This lesson says nothing about how any particular company packages or installs its product. In week 1, replace the generic nouns below with the real ones.

Words used here:
- **Image**: a frozen filesystem snapshot plus start command that a container runs from.
- **Registry**: a server that stores and serves images (and charts) by name.
- **Helm chart**: a package of templated Kubernetes config files that Helm installs with your settings filled in.
- **Pod**: Kubernetes' unit of running containers; **namespace**: a named partition of a cluster.
- **Air-gapped / disconnected**: a site with no network path to the outside.

## The problem and why it matters

An install is the first thing a customer sees, and it runs on a machine you have never seen, on a network you cannot reach, operated by someone who did not write your software. If it fails, you often get a screenshot and a vague description.

So packaging has one job: make the install *boring*. Ship everything the install needs, check the environment before changing it, make re-running safe, and fail with a message that names the cause. Most on-prem escalations in the first week are packaging problems (missing image, wrong driver, blocked network, not enough disk), not product bugs.

## First principles

1. **Ship the closure.** Everything the software needs to start must be in what you hand over, or listed as a prerequisite with a check. Any runtime download is a hidden dependency on the customer's network.
2. **Pin by digest, not by tag.** A tag (a human-readable label like `1.4.0`) can be moved to point at a different image. A digest (a fingerprint of the image's exact bytes, so the same digest always means the same image) cannot. Digests make "what is actually running" answerable.
3. **Check before you change.** A preflight is a read-only pass that reports every problem at once. It is far better than failing at step nine of twelve with half the system installed.
4. **Installs must be idempotent.** Running the installer twice must converge to the same state, because it will be re-run after partial failures.
5. **Fewer prerequisites, more adoption.** Each thing the customer must install first (a database, a message broker, which is a server that queues messages between programs, a particular OS) is a deal-breaker for someone. Bundle what you can; document the rest.

## How it works

### The shape of an artifact

```
 what you ship
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ release bundle (one version)         │
 │ ┌─────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  │
 │ │ images      │  │ chart / units  │  │
 │ │ (by digest) │  │ + default      │  │
 │ │             │  │   config       │  │
 │ └─────────────┘  └────────────────┘  │
 │ ┌─────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  │
 │ │ preflight + │  │ checksums +    │  │
 │ │ installer   │  │ signatures     │  │
 │ └─────────────┘  └────────────────┘  │
 └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The customer verifies the bundle, loads it, runs preflight, then installs. Treat the bundle as the unit of release: one version number covers images, chart and config together.

### Getting images into a disconnected environment

```
 vendor side            transfer         customer side
 ┌──────────┐  save   ┌─────────┐  load  ┌──────────┐
 │ registry │────────▶│ tar /   │───────▶│ internal │
 │  (yours) │  copy   │ dir on  │  push  │ mirror   │
 └──────────┘         │ media   │        │ registry │
                      └─────────┘        └────┬─────┘
                                              │ pull
                                         ┌────┴─────┐
                                         │ cluster  │
                                         └──────────┘
```

A tar is a single archive file holding many files. Two common tools (commands below were not run here; verify on your machine):

```bash
# Docker: write images to a tar, then load on the other side
docker save -o bundle-images.tar registry.example.com/app:1.4.0
docker load -i bundle-images.tar          # on the customer host

# skopeo: copy between registries or via a directory; --all copies every
# platform in a multi-arch image, not only the one matching this host
skopeo copy --all docker://registry.example.com/app:1.4.0 dir:./app-1.4.0
skopeo copy --all dir:./app-1.4.0 docker://mirror.internal/app:1.4.0
```

The `dir:` transport (a plain directory of manifest, layer files and signatures) is documented as a non-standardized format, primarily useful for debugging or inspection, so treat it as a transfer convenience, not a stable interchange format.

Helm charts can live in an OCI registry too (OCI is the standard image-and-artifact format that registries speak) (the same mirror), using `helm push mychart-0.1.0.tgz oci://host/helm-charts` and `helm install myrelease oci://host/helm-charts/mychart --version 0.1.0`. The customer's mirror registry then serves both images and chart. Your chart should let the customer set a single `image.registry` value so every image reference can be redirected to the mirror.

When a container sets no pull policy (the rule for when a node fetches an image), Kubernetes defaults to `IfNotPresent` if the image names a tag other than `latest`, and to `Always` if the tag is `latest` or omitted. If an image is missing locally and the registry is unreachable, the pod shows `ImagePullBackOff` (Kubernetes retries with a growing delay, capped at 5 minutes). Private registries need a pull secret: the Secrets in `imagePullSecrets` must exist in the same namespace as the Pod.

### Choosing a packaging format

| Format | Good for | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Helm chart on Kubernetes | Customers with a cluster; templated config; upgrade and rollback built in | You inherit "their cluster, their version"; chart values become your API |
| Docker Compose | Small single-host installs, trials | No rollback command in the `docker compose` CLI; one host is a single point of failure |
| systemd unit (Linux's service manager) with RPM/DEB (Linux package formats) | Bare metal or VMs without containers; strict hosts | You package per distro and manage library dependencies |
| VM image (OVA, AMI-like) | Customers who want an appliance (a pre-built, ready-to-run machine) | Large artifacts, OS patching becomes your problem |

A common pattern is Helm as the primary path and a single-node variant for trials. Whatever you choose, keep one config model underneath so support does not need to learn four.

### Hardware, drivers and sizing

A GPU workload (CUDA is NVIDIA's GPU programming platform; the driver is the OS software that talks to the GPU) has three layers that must agree: the **NVIDIA driver on the host**, the **CUDA runtime libraries your image carries**, and the **container runtime setup** (the NVIDIA Container Toolkit configures the container engine's runtime for GPUs).

- The NVIDIA driver is installed on the *host*. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit docs list it as a host prerequisite, along with a supported container engine, and the toolkit configures the engine's runtime.
- NVIDIA's CUDA compatibility documentation describes that applications can run across different driver versions: minor-version compatibility lets an application built within a CUDA major release family run on a sufficiently new driver (with possible feature limits), and a separate forward-compatibility package can let a newer toolkit run on an older driver where platform and GPU support allow. Treat the exact driver minimums as something you look up in NVIDIA's tables for your toolkit version; do not hard-code them from memory.
- **Sizing guidance** should be a table of *workload shapes to resources*, produced by measured runs (see `benchmarking-methodology`), with the hardware named. State clearly what was measured, and give customers a way to measure on their own hardware rather than trusting your numbers on theirs.

### Preflight and idempotent install

A preflight script reports every failing check, not just the first. Safe to run twice, makes no changes (tested on macOS with a failing DNS check, which is the point):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
fail=0
check() { name="$1"; shift
  if "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "PASS  $name"; else echo "FAIL  $name"; fail=1; fi; }
check "tar is available"          command -v tar
check "free disk on /tmp (example threshold 1 GiB)" \
  bash -c '[ "$(df -Pk /tmp | awk "NR==2{print \$4}")" -ge 1048576 ]'
check "can resolve registry name" \
  bash -c 'getent hosts registry.example.com || host registry.example.com'
exit $fail
```

For the install itself, `helm upgrade --install RELEASE CHART` is the idempotent form: it installs if the release does not exist and upgrades if it does. Useful flags from the Helm docs: `--values/-f` (repeatable, last file wins), `--dry-run` (with `client` or `server` mode), `--create-namespace`, `--wait` and `--timeout`, and `--wait-for-jobs` (wait for Jobs to finish). Failure rollback is `--atomic` in the Helm 3 docs (which also sets `--wait` automatically) and `--rollback-on-failure` in the Helm 4 docs (the Helm 4 `helm upgrade` page does not list `--atomic`); check which your customers' Helm version supports.

Ship **defaults that work with no edits** on a small footprint, plus a documented values file for production. A customer who gets to "healthy" in minutes will tolerate tuning later.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** the install at a customer's site finishes in the installer, but the main service pod has been `Pending` for twenty minutes.

1. **Read the pod's events** (`kubectl describe pod NAME`; `kubectl` is the Kubernetes command-line tool). Events say why it is not scheduled or started. Start here, always.
2. **Scheduler messages about insufficient CPU, memory or GPU in events:** the scheduler (the part of Kubernetes that picks a machine for each pod) cannot fit the pod. Compare requests to node capacity. A preflight that checked allocatable resources would have caught this.
3. **Waiting on a PersistentVolumeClaim** (a pod's request for disk storage)**:** the customer's cluster has no default storage class, or the class cannot provision. Ask which storage class they use.
4. **`ImagePullBackOff`:** the node cannot fetch the image. Is the image reference pointing at the mirror? Is there a pull secret? Is the registry's TLS certificate signed by a CA the node trusts?
5. **Pod started but crash-looping:** read the previous container's logs (`kubectl logs POD --previous`) and the exit state in `describe`.
6. **GPU pods stuck or failing with a driver error:** check the host driver is installed, the container runtime is configured for GPUs, and the node advertises a GPU resource.

**Fix:** per branch. Durable fix: move each of these checks into preflight, so the next customer sees "FAIL: no default storage class" before anything is installed, and make the installer's last step a post-install check that waits for health and prints the failing component's name.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| Helm on Kubernetes: customer already runs a cluster and wants standard tooling | Customer has no Kubernetes and no appetite to run one |
| Bundled dependencies: you need a simple install | Customer already operates the dependency and wants to bring their own (offer both) |
| Digest pinning and signed bundles: audited environments | Rapid trials where speed beats provenance (still sign production releases) |
| Appliance or VM: maximal control over the environment | You cannot take on OS patching and image size |

## Interview questions

1. Why pin an image by digest rather than tag? *Probe:* how would you roll out a fix, then? *Outline:* tags are movable pointers, digests are content hashes; a fix is a new image with a new digest referenced by a new release.
2. How would you deliver a release to a customer with no internet? *Probe:* what about the Helm chart? *Outline:* save or copy images to a tar or directory, transfer, push to an internal registry, chart in the same registry or as a file, verify checksums and signatures, no runtime downloads.
3. What belongs in a preflight check? *Outline:* tooling versions, CPU/memory/disk, storage class, network reachability (DNS, registry, proxies), time sync, GPU driver and runtime, permissions; read-only; reports all failures.
4. What does idempotent mean for an installer and why does it matter? *Outline:* re-running converges to the same state; partial failures are normal; use declarative apply, `upgrade --install`, no duplicate side effects.
5. How do GPU driver, CUDA and the container interact? *Probe:* where is the driver installed? *Outline:* host driver, CUDA libraries in the image, container runtime set up for GPUs; look up the compatibility matrix rather than guessing.
6. Helm vs Compose vs RPM/DEB: how do you choose? *Outline:* the table above, plus customer skills and upgrade needs.

**Worked exercise:** write a preflight checklist for installing a GPU-backed service on a customer's cluster. Mark which checks need cluster access, which need host access, and which the customer can run themselves without you.

## Checklist

1. I can explain why the artifact is a bundle with a single version.
2. I can describe two ways to get images into a disconnected site.
3. I can say why digests beat tags.
4. I can explain host driver vs CUDA runtime vs container runtime setup.
5. I can write a preflight and describe what makes an installer idempotent.

## Common wrong answers

- "The installer will download what it needs." Not in a disconnected site.
- "Use `latest`." Nobody can tell what is running, and rollbacks become guesses.
- "Install the GPU driver inside the container." The driver lives on the host.
- "If the install fails, retry." Without idempotency, retry may make it worse.

- https://helm.sh/docs/v3/helm/helm_upgrade/ (Helm 3.22.1): `--atomic` is listed ("rolls back changes made in case of failed upgrade", sets `--wait` automatically); `--rollback-on-failure` is not.

The `ErrImagePull` status name was not on any page I read, so it was removed.
- https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-pods/ : a Pending pod cannot be scheduled, usually for insufficient resources; look at `kubectl describe` for scheduler messages. https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes/ and https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/ : a claim with no class and no default StorageClass stays unset and unbound. https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/ : `kubectl describe pod` shows container state; a terminated container shows reason, exit code and times. https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_logs/ : `--previous`.
- https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/cuda-compatibility/index.html : minor-version compatibility (same major family, sufficiently new driver, some feature limitations) and forward compatibility (newer toolkit on older driver, subject to platform and GPU support). https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/container-toolkit/latest/install-guide.html : driver installed on the host (an inference from the install order), supported container engines, `nvidia-ctk runtime configure` edits the host engine config.

Commands run: the preflight script ran twice on macOS (tar and disk checks passed, the DNS check failed for the example hostname, exit 1 both times). Not run here: Docker (client installed, daemon not running), skopeo, Helm and kubectl commands, because none had a daemon, cluster or install available; their behavior rests on the docs above.
